claims.claim: pandas 3.0.2: read_csv drops leading zeros by default; int with None becomes float64; tz_localize rejects a nonexistent DST time.
Python 3.13: utcnow() raises a DeprecationWarning and is naive; comparing naive and aware datetimes raises TypeError.

PySpark 4.0.4: union matches by position; to_date depends on session time zone; naive strings parse relative to the session zone; ANSI casts a string compared with an int and raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT on 'x'.

concept_html:
Two more silent errors: values that change type, and times that change meaning with the zone.

Type coercion. Checked on pandas 3.0.2, PySpark 4.0.4 and Python 3.13:

  • pd.read_csv turns respondent_id 0123 into the integer 123. The leading zero is gone, and joins to the panel file fail. Pass dtype={"respondent_id": "string"} for identifiers.
  • An integer column with one missing value becomes float64 in pandas. 1 becomes 1.0, and string keys built from it read "1.0".
  • Strings sort as text: sorted(["10", "9", "2"]) gives ['10', '2', '9']. Wave "W10" sorts before "W2". Pad your ids, or sort on a number.
  • Spark's df.union(other) matches columns by position, not by name. A delivery with wave_id and respondent_id swapped unions without error, with the values in the wrong columns. Use unionByName.
  • Under ANSI mode, Spark casts a string column compared with a number: F.col("age") > 9 raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT on the value 'x'. Cast explicitly with try_cast first.

Timezone drift. A timestamp without a zone is a guess.

  • datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime and is deprecated from Python 3.12. Comparing naive with aware raises TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes. Use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
  • Spark's TIMESTAMP type is an instant, displayed in the session time zone (spark.sql.session.timeZone). F.to_date on 2026-06-30T23:30:00Z gives 30 June in UTC and 1 July in Europe/London. A wave cut-off at midnight moves respondents between waves.
  • The same text without an offset, '2026-06-30 23:30:00', parses to instants 4 hours apart in UTC and America/New_York sessions.
  • Some local times do not exist. pandas refuses to localise 2026-03-29 01:30 to Europe/London: the clocks skipped that hour.

Store instants in UTC. Convert to local time only for display, or for a business rule that names its zone, such as "fieldwork closes at midnight UK time".

exercises.prompt_html: Write load_delivery(csv_text: str) -> pd.DataFrame. Read the CSV with respondent_id and postcode_area as strings, keeping leading zeros. Convert final_weight to float. If any non-empty weight fails to parse, raise ValueError naming how many. Empty weights stay missing.
exercises.solution:
import io

import pandas as pd

ID_COLUMNS = {"respondent_id": "string", "postcode_area": "string"}


def load_delivery(csv_text: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a delivery CSV with identifiers as strings and weights as floats.

    Args:
        csv_text: CSV text with respondent_id, postcode_area and final_weight.

    Returns:
        The delivery as a DataFrame.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If any non-empty weight cannot be parsed.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text), dtype={**ID_COLUMNS, "final_weight": "string"})
    raw = df["final_weight"]
    parsed = pd.to_numeric(raw, errors="coerce")
    failed = int((raw.notna() & parsed.isna()).sum())
    if failed:
        raise ValueError(f"{failed} weights could not be parsed")
    return df.assign(final_weight=parsed.astype("float64"))

title: Type coercion and timezone drift
why_html: A wave closed at midnight UK time on 30 June. The pipeline ran with the session time zone set to UTC and assigned every interview completed between 23:00 and 00:00 UTC on 30 June to wave W14. In British Summer Time those interviews happened after midnight, in W15. 340 respondents moved wave. Both waves' reach figures shifted by up to 1.5 points.
